title: A series as a limit of partial sums
objectives: Define a series’ sum as the limit of its partial sums. Prove that terms of a convergent series tend to zero.

screens.title: Adding up the pieces
screens.prose: Take $\sum \tfrac{1}{n(n+1)} = \tfrac12 + \tfrac16 + \tfrac1{12} + \tfrac1{20} + \cdots$. The **partial sum** $S_n$ adds the first $n$ terms. Fill in four of them.

state.caption: Each dot rises to the $S_n$ you type.

screens.question: Fill in $S_1$ to $S_4$, as fractions or decimals.

hints.text: $S_1 = \tfrac12$ and $S_2 = \tfrac12 + \tfrac16$.
$\tfrac12 + \tfrac16 = \tfrac36 + \tfrac16 = \tfrac23$.
Add one term each time: $S_3 = \tfrac23 + \tfrac1{12} = \tfrac34$ and $S_4 = \tfrac34 + \tfrac1{20} = \tfrac45$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each partial sum is the one before plus the next term.

byKey.r1c1: Check $S_2$. If you typed the term $a_2$, that is one piece; $S_2$ adds every term up to $a_2$.
byKey.r2c1: Check $S_3$. If you typed the term $a_3$, that is one piece; $S_3$ adds every term up to $a_3$.
byKey.r3c1: Check $S_4$. If you typed the term $a_4$, that is one piece; $S_4$ adds every term up to $a_4$.

explain.text: The totals are $\tfrac12, \tfrac23, \tfrac34, \tfrac45$: each is $\tfrac{n}{n+1}$. Each falls short of 1 by $\tfrac{1}{n+1}$. The dots climb towards 1 and never reach it.

screens.title: A formula for $S_n$
screens.prose: Each term splits in two: $\tfrac{1}{k(k+1)} = \tfrac1k - \tfrac{1}{k+1}$. Added from $k = 1$ to $n$, the middle pieces cancel. Such a sum is **telescoping**, like the bound in Cauchy sequences.
screens.question: Give $S_n$ as a formula in $n$.

hints.text: Write $S_3 = (1 - \tfrac12) + (\tfrac12 - \tfrac13) + (\tfrac13 - \tfrac14)$.
Only the first piece, 1, and the last, $-\tfrac14$, survive.
In general the survivors are $1$ and $-\tfrac{1}{n+1}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write out the pieces for $n = 3$ and see which two survive.

byKey.last: You ended one place early. The last piece is $\tfrac1n - \tfrac{1}{n+1}$, so $-\tfrac{1}{n+1}$ survives. Check $n = 1$: $S_1 = \tfrac12$.
byKey.tail: You kept the last piece's part and lost the first. The 1 from $k = 1$ survives too.

screens.title: Inside every band
screens.prose: The dots are $S_n = 1 - \tfrac{1}{n+1}$ for $n$ up to 30. The band is $1 \pm \varepsilon$. Slide $\varepsilon$ and watch where the dots enter the band for good.

state.caption: $\varepsilon$ = 0.25: every $S_n$ from $n$ = 4 on lies inside the band.

frames.caption: $\varepsilon$ = 0.25: every $S_n$ from $n$ = 4 on lies inside the band.
$\varepsilon$ = 0.1: every $S_n$ from $n$ = 10 on lies inside the band.
$\varepsilon$ = 0.05: every $S_n$ from $n$ = 20 on lies inside the band.
$\varepsilon$ = 0.04: every $S_n$ from $n$ = 25 on lies inside the band.

screens.question: Now take $\varepsilon = 0.01$. What is the first $N$ with $|S_n - 1| < \varepsilon$ for every $n \ge N$?

hints.text: The gap is $|S_n - 1| = \tfrac{1}{n+1}$.
At $\varepsilon = 0.1$ the line sits at 10, because $\tfrac{1}{11} < 0.1$ while $\tfrac1{10}$ is not.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Solve $\tfrac{1}{n+1} < 0.01$ for the first whole $n$.

byKey.edge: At $n = 99$ the gap is $\tfrac{1}{100} = 0.01$ exactly. The band asks for strictly less.
byKey.sq: You took $\sqrt{100} = 10$, as if the gap were $\tfrac{1}{n^2}$. The gap here is $\tfrac{1}{n+1}$.

explain.text: $|S_n - 1| = \tfrac{1}{n+1} < 0.01$ exactly when $n + 1 > 100$, so $N = 100$. Every $\varepsilon$ has such an $N$, so $S_n \to 1$. That limit is what we will call the sum.

canvas.caption: $\varepsilon$ = 0.04: every $S_n$ from $n$ = 25 on lies inside the band.

screens.title: The sum of a series
screens.prose: For a series $\sum a_n$, the partial sums are $S_n = a_1 + \cdots + a_n$. If $S_n \to S$, the series **converges** and $$\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} a_n = \lim_{n \to \infty} S_n = S.$$ Otherwise it **diverges**. An infinite sum is a limit, not an addition.
screens.question: What is $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \tfrac{1}{n(n+1)}$?

options.why: You stopped at $S_{10}$. The sum is the limit of the $S_n$, not one of them.

options.text: It has no value: infinitely many terms cannot be added.
options.why: You read the sum as an endless addition. It is defined as $\lim S_n$, which exists here.
You expected positive terms to pile up for ever. Yet $S_n = 1 - \tfrac{1}{n+1} < 1$ for every $n$.

hints.text: The sum is $\lim S_n$.
$\tfrac{1}{n+1} \to 0$, so $S_n \to 1$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take the limit of $S_n = 1 - \tfrac{1}{n+1}$.

explain.text: $S_n = 1 - \tfrac{1}{n+1} \to 1$, so the series converges and its sum is 1. No partial sum equals 1. The sum is the limit, exactly as in level 2.

screens.title: Terms of a convergent series
screens.prose: Suppose $\sum a_n$ converges, with sum $S$. We prove that $a_n \to 0$. Two lines are flawed.
screens.question: Put the proof in order. Move the two flawed lines to Left out.

lines.text: $(S_{n-1})$ is $(S_n)$ shifted by one place, so $S_{n-1} \to S$ as well.
By the limit law for differences, $a_n \to S - S = 0$. $\blacksquare$
Since $a_n \to 0$, the partial sums settle, so $S_n \to S$.
lines.why: You argued the converse. Terms tending to 0 do not make $S_n$ converge, and it is not what we are proving.
You divided the total by $n$. That is the average term; $a_n$ is the step $S_n - S_{n-1}$.

hints.text: Write $a_n$ in terms of two partial sums.
Order: name the limit, then the difference and the shifted limit (either order), then the limit law.

feedback.correct: Right. A term is the difference of two partial sums with the same limit.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write $a_n = S_n - S_{n-1}$, then use the limit of each part.

byKey.d1: You argued from $a_n \to 0$. That is the conclusion, and the converse of what we prove.
byKey.d2: You used $\tfrac{S_n}{n}$. The term $a_n$ is $S_n - S_{n-1}$.
byKey.left-out: You left out a line the proof needs. Only the two flawed lines go to Left out.

explain.text: Each term is a step between neighbouring partial sums: $a_n = S_n - S_{n-1}$. Both sums tend to $S$. The difference law from level 2 gives $a_n \to 0$.

screens.title: The step that carries it
screens.prose: The proof said $S_{n-1} \to S$. Everything else is algebra or a limit law.
screens.question: Why is $S_{n-1} \to S$ true?

options.text: Both $S_n$ and $S_{n-1}$ tend to $S$: if $N$ works for $(S_n)$ and $\varepsilon$, then $N + 1$ works for $(S_{n-1})$.
$S_{n-1} < S_n$, so its limit is the smaller value $S - a_n$.
options.why: You let the limit depend on $n$. A limit is one number, and shifting a sequence one place does not change it.
You used the conclusion. We are proving $a_n \to 0$.
You assumed positive terms. Nothing here is monotone; the terms may have any signs.

hints.text: $(S_{n-1})$ is the list $S_1, S_2, S_3, \dots$ started one place later.
If $|S_n - S| < \varepsilon$ for all $n \ge N$, what about $|S_{n-1} - S|$?
For $n \ge N + 1$, $n - 1 \ge N$, so $|S_{n-1} - S| < \varepsilon$.

feedback.correct: Right. Shifting an index does not change a limit.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the lists $(S_n)$ and $(S_{n-1})$ term by term.

explain.text: For $n \ge N + 1$ we have $n - 1 \ge N$, so $|S_{n-1} - S| < \varepsilon$. So $(S_{n-1})$ has the same limit $S$. The difference $a_n = S_n - S_{n-1}$ then tends to 0.

screens.title: The term test
screens.prose: Turned round, the theorem reads: if $a_n \not\to 0$, then $\sum a_n$ diverges. Try $\sum \tfrac{n}{n+1} = \tfrac12 + \tfrac23 + \tfrac34 + \cdots$. The dots are its terms.
screens.question: What does the term test say about $\sum \tfrac{n}{n+1}$?

options.text: It converges: the terms are bounded by 1.
options.why: You bounded the terms, not the sums. Terms near 1 add about 1 each time, so $S_n \ge \tfrac n2$.

options.text: Nothing: the term test cannot prove divergence.
options.why: You read the test backwards. It never proves convergence, but it does prove divergence when $a_n \not\to 0$.

options.text: It converges to 1, the limit of the terms.
options.why: You took the terms' limit for the sum. The sum is the limit of $S_n$, and $S_n \ge \tfrac n2$.

hints.text: Where do the dots head?
$\tfrac{n}{n+1} \to 1$.
A convergent series has $a_n \to 0$. Here $a_n \to 1$.

feedback.correct: Right. The terms do not tend to 0, so the series diverges.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the limit of the terms, then use the theorem in its contrapositive form.

explain.text: Every term is at least $\tfrac12$, so $S_n \ge \tfrac n2$, which is unbounded. The term test says it in one line: $a_n \to 1 \ne 0$. The test only ever proves divergence.

screens.title: The converse fails
screens.prose: The terms of $\sum \tfrac1n$ tend to 0. Group them in blocks that double: $$1 + \tfrac12 + \left(\tfrac13 + \tfrac14\right) + \left(\tfrac15 + \cdots + \tfrac18\right) + \cdots$$ The table sets $S_{2^k}$ beside $1 + \tfrac k2$.
screens.question: What lower bound does the grouping give for $S_{1024}$?

hints.text: Each bracket has twice as many terms as the one before.
The bracket from $\tfrac15$ to $\tfrac18$ has 4 terms, each at least $\tfrac18$: at least $\tfrac12$.
$1024 = 2^{10}$: the first term plus 10 blocks of at least $\tfrac12$ each.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write 1024 as a power of 2 and read the pattern in the last column.

byKey.no-one: You counted the blocks but dropped the first term, 1. The bound is $1 + \tfrac{10}{2}$.
byKey.halves: You halved the number of terms. Each block adds at least $\tfrac12$, and there are only 10 blocks.
byKey.true: That is the true value, $S_{1024} \approx 7.5092$. The grouping proves the weaker bound $1 + \tfrac{10}{2}$.

explain.text: Block $j$ has $2^{j-1}$ terms, each at least $\tfrac{1}{2^j}$, so it adds at least $\tfrac12$. So $S_{1024} \ge 1 + \tfrac{10}{2} = 6$, while in fact $S_{1024} \approx 7.5092$. The bound $1 + \tfrac k2$ has no ceiling.

screens.title: The harmonic series diverges
screens.prose: Now the grouping as a proof. Block $j$ runs from $\tfrac{1}{2^{j-1} + 1}$ to $\tfrac{1}{2^j}$. Two lines are flawed.
screens.question: Put the proof in order. Move the two flawed lines to Left out.

lines.text: Each term of block $j$ is at least $\tfrac{1}{2^j}$, so the block adds at least $2^{j-1} \cdot \tfrac{1}{2^j} = \tfrac12$.
$S_{2^k}$ is 1 plus blocks 1 to $k$, so $S_{2^k} \ge 1 + \tfrac k2$.
So $(S_n)$ is unbounded. A convergent sequence is bounded, so $\sum \tfrac1n$ diverges. $\blacksquare$
Each term of block $j$ is at most $\tfrac{1}{2^{j-1}}$, so each block adds at most 1.
lines.why: You bounded the blocks from above. An upper bound cannot show that the sums grow.

lines.text: The terms $\tfrac1n$ tend to 0, so the blocks tend to 0.
lines.why: You let small terms make small blocks. Block $j$ has $2^{j-1}$ terms, and their total stays at least $\tfrac12$.

hints.text: Count the terms in a block, then bound each one from below.
The smallest term in block $j$ is its last, $\tfrac{1}{2^j}$.
Order: count, bound each block, add the blocks, conclude from unboundedness.

feedback.correct: Right. Each block adds at least a half, for ever.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count a block's terms, bound the block below by $\tfrac12$, then add the blocks.

byKey.d1: You used an upper bound. To show divergence, the blocks need a lower bound.
byKey.d2: You let the blocks shrink with the terms. Each block has more terms, and adds at least $\tfrac12$.
byKey.left-out: You left out a line the proof needs. Only the two flawed lines go to Left out.

explain.text: Each block adds at least $\tfrac12$, so $S_{2^k} \ge 1 + \tfrac k2$, which passes any bound. Unbounded partial sums cannot converge. So $a_n \to 0$ is needed for convergence, but it is not enough.

screens.title: Brackets that lie
screens.prose: A classmate writes $1 - 1 + 1 - 1 + \cdots = (1 - 1) + (1 - 1) + \cdots = 0$. Another brackets from the second term and gets 1. The dots are the partial sums.
screens.question: What is $1 - 1 + 1 - 1 + \cdots$?

options.text: It diverges: $S_n$ runs $1, 0, 1, 0, \dots$ with no limit, and the terms do not tend to 0.

options.why: You inserted brackets in pairs. That keeps only $S_2, S_4, \dots$, and the odd partial sums sit at 1.
Your brackets keep only $S_1, S_3, S_5, \dots$. The even partial sums are all 0.

options.text: $\tfrac12$, the average of the two values.
options.why: You averaged the partial sums. The sum is $\lim S_n$, and $(S_n)$ has no limit.

hints.text: The sum is the limit of the partial sums. Read them off the dots.
$S_n$ is 1 for odd $n$ and 0 for even $n$.
A sequence with two strands, at 0 and at 1, has no limit.

feedback.correct: Right. Brackets chose a subsequence; the sequence itself has no limit.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what the dots, all of them, tend to.

byKey.zero: You bracketed in pairs. That picks the subsequence $S_2, S_4, \dots$; a subsequence can settle when the sequence does not.

explain.text: Brackets pick out a subsequence of $(S_n)$: the even sums, all 0, or the odd ones, all 1. Two strands with different limits mean no limit, as in level 2. The term test agrees at once: $(-1)^{n+1} \not\to 0$.

screens.title: Partial sums as code
screens.prose: Write `first_exceeding(t)`, the smallest $n$ with $H_n = 1 + \tfrac12 + \cdots + \tfrac1n > t$, and `telescoping_sum(n)`, the $S_n$ of $\sum \tfrac{1}{k(k+1)}$ as an exact `Fraction`.
screens.question: Complete both functions.

widget.starter:
from fractions import Fraction

def first_exceeding(t):
    """Smallest n with H_n = 1 + 1/2 + ... + 1/n > t."""
    ...

def telescoping_sum(n):
    """S_n of the series 1/(k(k+1)) as an exact Fraction."""
    ...

tests.call: all(telescoping_sum(n) == 1 - Fraction(1, n + 1) for n in range(1, 40))

widget.how: Check runs 13 hidden tests, all compared exactly. Eight check first_exceeding. They include t = 10 and the strict cases t = 1 and t = 1.5, where H_1 and H_2 equal t. Five check telescoping_sum, including that it returns a Fraction equal to 1 - 1/(n + 1) up to n = 39.

hints.text: Keep a running total and a counter; stop as soon as the total passes $t$.
The loop condition is `total <= t`, because we need $H_n > t$ strictly.
For the other function, add `Fraction(1, k * (k + 1))` for `k` from 1 to `n`.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the strict inequality in `first_exceeding` and keep `telescoping_sum` in `Fraction`.

explain.text: $H_n$ passes 2, 3, 4 and 5 at $n = 4$, 11, 31 and 83, and 10 at 12367. They diverge, but about as slowly as $\ln n$. The telescoping sums are exactly $\tfrac{n}{n+1}$, so they never pass 1.

screens.title: Pricing a share by its dividends
screens.prose: A share pays £5 next year, growing 3% a year. Investors discount at 8%. Its price is $$\sum_{n \ge 1} \frac{5 \times 1.03^{n-1}}{1.08^n} = \frac{5}{0.08 - 0.03} = \text{£}100.$$ The bars show what each of the first ten dividends is worth today.
screens.question: How much of the £100 do the first ten dividends supply? Give pounds to the penny.

hints.text: This is $S_{10}$ of a geometric series.
First term $\tfrac{5}{1.08} \approx 4.63$, ratio $r = \tfrac{1.03}{1.08} \approx 0.9537$.

feedback.correct: Right. About £37.75, under two fifths of the price.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the ten discounted values, or use $S_{10} = 100(1 - r^{10})$.

byKey.raw: You added ten payments of £5. They grow, and each must be discounted to today.
byKey.grown: You grew the dividends but did not discount them. Divide year $n$'s payment by $1.08^n$.
byKey.flat: You used the first year's £4.63 for all ten years. Each later value is $\tfrac{1.03}{1.08}$ of the one before.

explain.text: $S_{10} = 100(1 - 0.6225) = \text{£}37.75$, the sum of the bars; most of the price lies beyond year 10. The infinite sum exists because the ratio is below 1. At 8% growth each term stays near £4.63, so the series diverges and gives no price.

ideas: A series converges when its partial sums $S_n$ converge; the sum is $\lim S_n$. Telescoping gives $\sum \tfrac{1}{n(n+1)} = 1$.
Term test: if $\sum a_n$ converges then $a_n = S_n - S_{n-1} \to 0$. So $a_n \not\to 0$ proves divergence.
The converse fails: grouping gives $S_{2^k} \ge 1 + \tfrac k2$, so $\sum \tfrac1n$ diverges although $\tfrac1n \to 0$.

formula.name: Sum of a series
formula.note: Changing finitely many terms can change the sum, never whether it converges.

summary.trap: Brackets choose a subsequence of $(S_n)$: $(1 - 1) + (1 - 1) + \cdots = 0$ says nothing about $1 - 1 + 1 - \cdots$, which diverges.

quiz.prose: Replace the first three terms of $\sum \tfrac{1}{n(n+1)}$ by 5, 5 and 5, and keep every later term.
quiz.question: What happens to the series?

options.why: You kept the old sum. The first three terms changed by $15 - \tfrac34$, and so does every later $S_n$.

options.text: It diverges, because the first terms are no longer small.
options.why: You let three terms decide. From $n = 4$ on nothing changed, and convergence depends only on the tail.

options.text: We cannot tell without recomputing every $S_n$.
options.why: For $n \ge 3$, each new $S_n$ is the old one plus $15 - \tfrac34$. So the limit moves by that amount.

feedback.correct: Right. The sum moves; convergence does not.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare each new partial sum with the old one from $n = 3$ on.

explain.text: The old terms $\tfrac12 + \tfrac16 + \tfrac1{12} = \tfrac34$ become 15. From $n = 3$ on, every $S_n$ rises by $15 - \tfrac34 = 14.25$, so the limit is $1 + 14.25 = 15.25$. Changing finitely many terms can change the sum, never whether it converges.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Subtract the first four terms, $S_4$, from the whole sum.

byKey.early: You subtracted $S_3 = \tfrac34$. The tail from $n = 5$ leaves out four terms, so subtract $S_4$.
byKey.late: You subtracted $S_5 = \tfrac56$. That removes the $n = 5$ term, which the tail includes.

explain.text: The tail from $n = 5$ is $1 - S_4 = 1 - \tfrac45 = \tfrac15$. Telescoping gives it directly: the pieces from $\tfrac15 - \tfrac16$ on leave only $\tfrac15$. Both routes agree.

quiz.prose: In the dividend model, suppose growth rises to the discount rate: £5 next year, growing 8%, discounted at 8%.
quiz.question: What does the series say about the price?

options.text: There is no price: every term equals $\tfrac{5}{1.08} \approx \text{£}4.63$, so the terms do not tend to 0 and the series diverges.
The price is $\tfrac{5}{0.08 - 0.08}$, which is very large but finite.
options.why: You divided by zero. The formula came from a geometric sum with ratio below 1, which no longer holds.
You kept the old answer. With equal rates each term is £4.63, and $S_n \approx 4.63n$.

options.text: It converges, because each term is discounted.
options.why: You trusted the discounting. Here the growth cancels it exactly, so no term shrinks.

feedback.correct: Right. The term test rules the series out.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out a typical term with equal rates.

explain.text: Each term is $\tfrac{5 \times 1.08^{n-1}}{1.08^n} = \tfrac{5}{1.08}$, the same every year. The terms tend to £4.63, not 0, so the series diverges. The formula $\tfrac{5}{r - g}$ is valid only when $g < r$.

quiz.question: What are its terms and its sum?

options.why: You summed $\tfrac{1}{n(n-1)}$ from $n = 2$, which gives 1, and lost $a_1 = S_1 = 1$. The sum is $\lim S_n = 2$.
You read $S_n$ as the term. The terms are the steps $S_n - S_{n-1}$.
You guessed the terms. $S_2 - S_1 = \tfrac32 - 1 = \tfrac12$, not $\tfrac14$.

feedback.correct: Right. Terms are differences of partial sums.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use $a_n = S_n - S_{n-1}$ and $\sum a_n = \lim S_n$.

explain.text: $a_1 = S_1 = 1$ and, for $n \ge 2$, $a_n = \tfrac{1}{n-1} - \tfrac1n = \tfrac{1}{n(n-1)}$. The sum is $\lim (2 - \tfrac1n) = 2$. Check: $a_n \to 0$, as the term test requires.
